title: Adjectives and double definiteness
goal: Use adjectives in all three forms, master double definiteness, and describe people and things.
bekal: use double definiteness: *den store bil*, not *den store bilen*
wave: Review **unit 13** first: make ten sentences using all five modal verbs, five of them negative. Double-check what *må ikke* means.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Han står ved indgangen
dialogs.intro: Mette is picking up her cousin at the station, but they've never met. She calls Budi, who is already there.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Budi, kan du se ham? Han skulle stå ved indgangen.
lines.id: Budi, can you see him? He's supposed to be standing by the entrance.
lines.literal: Budi, can you see him? he should stand by entrance-the.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Han er høj og tynd. Og han har en rød jakke på.
lines.id: He's tall and thin. And he's wearing a red jacket.
lines.literal: he is tall and thin. and he has a red jacket on.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Der står to høje mænd. Én med rød jakke, én med sort.
lines.id: There are two tall men. One in a red jacket, one in black.
lines.literal: there stand two tall men. one with red jacket, one with black.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Har den røde jakke en stor rygsæk?
lines.id: Does the red jacket have a big backpack?
lines.literal: has the red jacket a big backpack?

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Det er ham. Han har altid den grimmeste rygsæk i familien.
lines.id: That's him. He always has the ugliest backpack in the family.
lines.literal: it is him. he has always the ugliest backpack in family-the.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Han ser meget venlig ud. Skal jeg sige noget?
lines.id: He looks very friendly. Shall I say something?
lines.literal: he sees very friendly out. shall I say something?

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Ja, sig at hans kusine kommer om fem minutter.
lines.id: Yes, tell him his cousin will be there in five minutes.
lines.literal: yes, say that his cousin comes in five minutes.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Fem minutter i dansk tid, eller fem minutter i rigtig tid?
lines.id: Five minutes in Danish time, or five minutes in real time?
lines.literal: five minutes in Danish time, or five minutes in real time?

notes: **Hvordan ser han ud?** = "what does he look like?" *At se ud* is a phrasal verb, and the *ud* part stands far back: *Han ser meget venlig **ud**.* Everything describing him slips in between — like English "look *him* up".
**Han har en rød jakke på** — *at have på* = to be wearing. Same pattern: *på* gets thrown to the end. Compare *at tage på* (to put on, as an action): *Jeg tager min jakke på.*
**Den røde jakke** — notice three things at once: *den* in front, the adjective ending in *-e*, and *jakke* **without** the *-n* ending. This is double definiteness, and it's the heart of this unit.
**Kæmpestor** = huge. The prefix *kæmpe-* (giant) can be stuck onto any adjective to exaggerate: *kæmpestor*, *kæmpegodt*, *kæmpedyrt*. Very colloquial and very useful.
**Den grimmeste** = the ugliest. The superlative always takes *den/det/de* in front and ends in *-e*: *den største*, *det bedste*, *de flotteste*.
**Sig** is the command form of *at sige* — don't confuse it with the reflexive *sig* from unit 9. Two words spelled exactly the same, with very different meanings, and context keeps them apart.
**Frækt sagt** = "cheeky thing to say". *Fræk* means naughty, cheeky, sometimes flirty — a word with a wide range, often used jokingly.
**Dansk tid** — an inside joke. The opposite is actually true: Danish time means being on time. Budi is joking by turning it around.

grammars.title: The three forms of an adjective
body: Danish adjectives have only three forms, and the rule for choosing can be boiled down to three lines.
after: The last three rows boil down to one sentence: **if the noun is already definite, the adjective always takes -e.** Singular or plural, en-word or et-word — doesn't matter.

Exceptions to learn: adjectives already ending in **-t**, **-sk** or **-ed** don't add another *t* — *et sort bord*, *et dansk hus*, *et lukket vindue*. Adjectives ending in a vowel don't either: *et blå hus*, but *et nyt hus* (an exception to the exception — *ny* does add *t*).
Adjectives ending in **-el, -en, -er** drop the middle *e* when adding *-e*: *gammel → gamle*, *sulten → sultne*, *lækker → lækre*.

grammars.title: Double definiteness
body: This is a structure English doesn't have, and at first it often feels like overkill.
The rule: **as soon as there's an adjective, the article moves to the front as a separate word, and the noun loses its ending.**
after: ⚠️ **Den store bilen** is wrong. The ending is dropped as soon as *den* appears. This is the opposite of Norwegian and Swedish, which keep both — so if you've touched those languages, be careful.
If the noun stays indefinite, nothing changes at all: *en stor bil* (a big car).
The last row shows that *lille* stays *lille* — it's one of the few adjectives that never adds anything in the singular. Its plural is a different word: *små*.

grammars.title: Comparing
body: Two endings, and a small group of rebellious words — much like English *bigger, biggest* and *better, best*.
after: Long adjectives — usually more than two syllables and of foreign origin — use *mere* and *mest* instead of endings, just like English *more* and *most*.
The word for "than" is **end**: *Han er højere **end** mig.* For equality: *lige så høj **som** mig* (as tall as me).
The superlative always takes *den/det/de* when it describes a noun: *den bedste bog*. Standing alone after *er*, it's bare: *Den bog er bedst.*

blocks.text: *Sød* is used much more widely than English "sweet": for people (kind), for children (adorable), for taste (sweet), and for actions (*hvor sødt af dig!* = how kind of you!).

Colors: *rød* (red), *blå* (blue), *grøn* (green), *gul* (yellow), *sort* (black), *hvid* (white), *grå* (gray), *brun* (brown), *lyserød* (pink), *lilla* (purple). Notice that *sort*, *hvid* and *lilla* don't add *t* for et-words.

sections.title: Pattern drill: one adjective, four situations

blocks.text: Read each row in full from left to right, out loud. This is the fastest way to move the rule into your ear.

blocks.title: The most common mistakes
items: **Forgetting -t for et-words.** *Et stor hus* — the number one mistake, because the ear doesn't always catch the difference.
**Adding the ending after den.** *Den store bilen* — carried over from Norwegian or from the logic "more definite is better".
**Forgetting -e in the plural.** *To stor huse* — easy to miss when speaking fast.
None of the three get in the way of understanding, but all three are clearly audible. The good news: they disappear by drilling the table above, not by rereading the rules.

items: He is wearing a red jacket.
This book is better than that one.
She is the youngest in the family.
